items: On the fourth evening, they came with their children. Fathers who had heard the first songs wanted witnesses.
Sing the judgment, father. Though I find I am half afraid of it now.
You are right to be, child. Tonight a herdsman chooses among three goddesses — and every man and woman in this hall is living yet inside his choice.
Muse, sing through me the judgment on Ida: three queens of heaven, one apple of gold, and the most dangerous prize ever offered to a mortal man.
Hear then, as the Muse gives it.
On the mountain, the piping had stopped. The lights had come to the fire.
Even the cattle knelt. Alexandros the herdsman covered his eyes and waited to die.
Stand up, son of the mountain. You are not to die — you are to judge. Zeus commands it: no god will harm you, whatever you decide. Though I would not envy you either way.
This gold says: FOR THE FAIREST. These three claim it. Zeus refuses to choose. You — the fairest judge among mortals — will give it to one of them.
So the fairness of a bull-ring came home to roost. Be careful, princes, what you become known for. Heaven takes note — and heaven delegates.
Look at me first, herdsman, and hear me. I am the queen of heaven.
Give me the gold, and I give you lordship: all Asia under your throne, kings for your servants, no city closed to you. Power, herdsman — the first and last of prizes.
And the herdsman, who had never owned more than a staff, looked at all the kingdoms of the earth.
Now hear me, son of Priam.
She named his blood before his blood was known. The grey-eyed one wastes nothing — not even a secret.
Give me the gold, and I give you the two things no man keeps long: victory in every battle, and wisdom in every counsel. You will never be beaten and never be a fool.
This was the better gift. Every wise head in this hall knows it was the better gift. Hold that thought.
They offer you thrones and armies, sweet judge. Heavy things. I offer one thing only — and it weighs nothing at all.
The most beautiful woman the sun has ever seen — Helen of Sparta. Give me the gold, and she is yours: your wife, your own, though the whole world stand between you.

She did not mention that Helen was already a wife, already a queen, already the hinge of a sworn oath binding every king in Greece. Gods bargain like merchants, princes: the flaw is never in the listing.
And Alexandros gave the gold to Aphrodite.

Weigh it fairly, princes, before you despise him: he was young, and alone, and it was the goddess of desire herself desiring to win. But weigh also this: in that minute were born the two immortal hatreds — Hera's and Athena's — that will not sleep now until Troy is ash. Not hatred of Paris only. Hatred of Troy, root and branch, wall and cradle. Such is the arithmetic of heaven: one man's choice, one city's bill.
Rise, judge. What I promised, I perform. But a herdsman cannot woo a queen of Greece.
First, be known. Go down to the city at the games, and let your blood declare itself. You are no herdsman's son — but that is Troy's tale to tell you, not mine.
And she left him with a promise, a mystery, and a road pointing down the mountain. He took the road. Every step of the rest of this song is that road.
That season, the king's men came up the mountain to take beasts for the great games at Troy — the games King Priam held every year in memory of a son long dead. They took the best bull on Ida.
Then I will go to their games — and win him back.
Boy — hear me once. Do not shine too bright down there. Some fires, once lit... [he cannot finish]
The old man knew what he had never told. And he let him go anyway. Ask the fathers in this hall how that is possible. They know.
At the games, an unknown herdsman entered every contest — and won every contest. He outran the princes. He outboxed the princes.
And the king and queen looked at the shining stranger, and something older than memory turned over in both their hearts.
A slave from the hills does not shame the sons of Priam! Your blood will answer it!
And in one breath the feast became a blade — for the pride of princes is dry tinder. He spoke of blood. He was about to learn whose.
STOP! Strike him and you strike your own house — he is your BROTHER! He is the child of the dream — the son that was cast away!
It is truth, my king. I could not do it. The bear nursed him — the gods kept him — I raised him... Forgive an old man. This is your son.
Alive. Alive. The gods have given back what I paid... My son. My son Alexandros.
And there was such joy in Troy that day as the city had never known. Hold the joy, princes. Look at it well. It is real joy — and it is the door standing open.
They bathed him and robed him and set him between the king and queen, and the princes embraced their brother — Hector first and most truly, as Hector did all things.
You are feasting the FIREBRAND! The dream was TRUE — the fire is IN THE HOUSE — put it out, father, put it out while it is still small —!
Peace, child, peace. The gods kept him alive against my own decree — the doom is annulled, the debt is paid. Let the house rejoice.
So the one true voice was led from the hall — kindly, which is worse. The dream was not annulled, princes. It was only postponed. Heaven does not forget; it reschedules.
They forgot the dream, father? A dream that made a king cast out his own son — forgotten in a day?

Not forgotten, child. Overruled. Joy is a strong wine, and relief is a stronger one — and a doom postponed feels exactly like a doom escaped. Exactly like it. There is no feeling in the world more dangerous.
Now the goddess collects her judge. A ship is building at the shore.
Phereclus the craftsman built the ships — well-made, fatal ships. The singer of the great war will pause one day, in the middle of the battle, to remember with sorrow the man who built them.
Do not let this fleet sail, father. I have seen its homecoming: it returns with fire in the hold. My sister and I have seen one seeing.
It is an embassy, Helenus — gifts and greetings to the kings of Greece, no more. Shall I cage the son heaven gave back? Sail, Alexandros — and sail home swiftly.
Twice warned, princes. Count the warnings as we go. Heaven's ledger does; and the price of each one refused is added to the bill.
So Alexandros sailed for Greece, and with him went his kinsman Aeneas of Dardania — a pious, steady young man, who will outlive everyone in this story. Mark him.
An embassy, cousin. Gifts and greetings. Tell me that is all this is.
It is what the goddess wills it to be, Aeneas. I have stopped steering. I sailed the day I judged.
He spoke truer than he knew. Whether that excuses him, the songs argue to this day — and so will you, princes, before I am done with you.
And Menelaus king of Sparta received the prince of Troy as guest-law commands: with open gates, with the best of the house, with the wrist-clasp of trust.
*GUEST-LAW (xenia) — the sacred bond of host and guest, watched over by Zeus himself. To harm one's host — or rob him — was among the deepest crimes the age knew.
Nine days Menelaus feasted him. Gifts were given and received. Every rite of the guest-bond was performed to the letter — by the host.
And at the hearth sat the queen.
He had seen her once already, in a goddess's golden mist. The mist had not lied.
And Helen looked back — once — and did not know why. The songs are careful here, princes, and I will be careful with them.

For this was not two mortals glancing across a fire. The third figure in that hall was a goddess, and she was working. What Helen chose and what was chosen FOR her, no singer has ever fully unwoven. Homer himself, when he comes to her, will not condemn her. Neither will I.

This is what the feast truly looked like, if mortal eyes could see: a goddess paying a debt with other people's lives. She had promised the judge the most beautiful woman in the world. That the woman was a wife, a queen, and the guarded treasure of a sworn oath — that was not the goddess's concern. Gods keep their promises, princes. It is one of the most dangerous things about them.
Then word came that Menelaus's grandsire had died in Crete, and the rites called him — a duty no king could refuse.
Keep the house, my queen, and keep our guests in all honor till I return. [to Paris] The house is yours, prince of Troy — as if I stood in it.

"As if I stood in it." He gave his trust whole, as the law commands the host to give it. Remember, when the war comes, who kept the law and who broke it. The whole of Greece will remember. They swore to.

On that night, the goddess came to the queen — no shimmer now, but seated at her hearth like kin. What was said, no song records. What the goddess is, every song records: she is the power that unmakes resolve. Mortals do not wrestle her and win. Peleus wrestled a sea-nymph; no one wrestles Aphrodite.

And they did not go empty-handed. The treasure of Menelaus's house went aboard with his queen — the theft sealed to the betrayal, so that no kindness could ever be argued of it. Aeneas kept the ships that night, and kept his silence, and was ashamed. The songs remember that too.

And Helen of Sparta went aboard the Trojan ship. Compelled, or consenting, or some third thing between that has no name — I told you the songs do not unweave it, and I will not lie to you by pretending they do. She looked back once. Then the ship took her. And somewhere in the dark of Greece, an oath began to wake.
They were two days out when the sky broke. Hera sent it — her first installment. It scattered the fleet and drove them far off course.
And in the thunder some swore they saw a crowned shape, watching. Not striking — watching. The queen of heaven is in no hurry. She has a whole war to spend.
By strange coasts and long delays — the songs name Sidon of the purple cloth — the ships came at last to the one harbor in the world they should never have entered.
So Alexandros brought Helen of Sparta home to Troy. And the city that came to stare fell silent as she passed — and then, being human, it cheered.
TAKE HER BACK! Ships — I see ships like a forest on the sea — take her back, take her BACK —
Third warning, princes. The ledger notes it. The crowd cheered louder.
Send her home, my king, with the treasure and an indemnity, and this can still be paid in gold instead of sons.
...She has eaten at my hearth, Antenor. She is under my roof and my guest-law now. And done is done. Troy does not hand a suppliant woman back like a strayed heifer.

Both men were right, by the two laws they lived by — that is the tragedy, and I will not cheapen it. But mark: with those words, one man's theft became the whole city's keeping. The bill was countersigned.
And Menelaus came home from his grandsire's grave to a cold hearth, an emptied treasury, and a gone wife.
He did not shout. Men who shout are asking the world to argue with them. He had nothing left to argue.
Ride to Mycenae. Tell my brother. Tell him... the oath.

Two words, princes. With two words the seed that Odysseus planted at the horse-sacrifice broke the earth at last. Every king who swore now owed his sword. The reckoning of the wedding-court had begun.
But father — her BROTHERS! Castor and Polydeuces tore down a fortress when she was a child! Thieves in the night — they would have had her back before the sails were dry!

Sit, child. You ask the very question Helen will ask herself, years from now, standing on the walls of Troy and searching the Greek host for two faces she will never find. Homer himself will give her that moment. And the answer is the saddest small song inside this great one.
While Paris sailed, the sons of the egg fought their last fight. Hear how the Dioscuri ended.

There was an old quarrel between the sons of Tyndareus and their cousins of Messene — Idas the strong and Lynceus of the far sight — over cattle, and honor, and the shares of a raid gone sour. That autumn it came to iron.
Castor lay in wait in a hollow oak, as raiders do.
But no tree in Greece was proof against the eyes of Lynceus, who could see through oak and earth and stone. He saw. He pointed. And Idas threw.
The spear went through the oak, and through the raider in it. Castor — the horseman, the mortal-born — took his death-wound in a cattle-feud, in the dark, far from any glory.
Polydeuces avenged him in the time it takes to say it: Lynceus fell to his hands, and Zeus himself took Idas with the bolt — for the god would not let the slayer of his son's brother see morning.
Brother... it is dark early tonight...
And Polydeuces the deathless held his dying brother, and discovered what immortality is for: it is for outliving.
Polydeuces, my son. Your brother was mortal-got; his thread is cut. But you are mine: rise and come — Olympus is open to you, whole and forever.
Whole and forever — without him? Father, what would I do there? Halve it. Whatever I am, halve it. Give my brother half my heaven and give me half his grave.

And Zeus — who refuses nearly everything — granted it. Day about, the songs say: one day both beneath the earth in Lacedaemon, one day both among the stars. The Twins you steer by, sailors of this hall, are that bargain kept. It is the one wholly honorable thing in tonight's whole song. Naturally, it is also the saddest.

So when the summons of the oath went out through Greece, no ship came from the brothers of Helen. The hearth of Tyndareus had gone dark in a single season: two daughters carried to two dooms, two sons to the earth and the sky.

And years from now — Homer has promised it, and I keep his promises — Helen on the wall of Troy will search the whole Greek host for her brothers, and wonder aloud why they alone have not come to fight for her: whether they were ashamed of her. She will get no answer.

For the life-giving earth already held them, there in their own dear country. That is the whole verse, princes, almost as the great singer will make it. I give it to you early, so that when you hear it in its place, you will know why it is the tenderest knife in the Iliad.
A cattle-feud. The rescuers of Aphidna — finished by a cattle-feud while their sister was stolen. Father, is heaven MOCKING us?

No, child. Heaven is TIMING us. The one sword that could have cut this knot quietly was removed from the board in the same season the knot was tied. Call it chance, and sleep well. Call it the plan of Zeus, and understand the song. I have never been able to tell you which — only that the songs allow both, always both.
And so nothing now stands between the theft and the reckoning. The oath is waking in every hall in Greece.
Enough. The apple is given. The queen is taken. The brothers are stars. The oath is awake.

Tomorrow the kings gather, child. Tomorrow: a madman's plow at Ithaca, an omen of a serpent and nine sparrows, a thousand ships at Aulis — and a war that begins by striking the wrong country entirely. Sleep while you can.
"Zeus of the Guest-Table walks unseen beside every stranger. The man who wrongs the host whose bread he has eaten — that man has the Avengers for fellow-travelers, all the days of his life."
— after the faith of the songs concerning the god of host and guest.
